title: A short-table scan declared as the intended change, whose proof covers no table at the default bound
summary: The interpreter's `lookupswitch` search gains a linear scan for tables of at most eight pairs, and the regression proof is asked to show the bisection unchanged on the rest: `--unchanged-unless 'matches.length <= 8'`. The default bound on array parameters is eight, so every table in the domain is among the intended inputs, the harness returns before calling either version, and the proof covers no input. The verdict is verified, vacuously, and the tool says so on a line of its own, found by running the statement with the calls replaced by the assertion's failure.

change.description: A table of at most `SCAN_LIMIT` (eight) pairs is scanned in order, `for (int i = 0; i < matches.length; i++) if (matches[i] == key) return i;`, and the bisection is kept for longer tables as it was. The tests for the bisection pass.

risk: None in the code: the scan agrees with the bisection on every sorted table (example 145's notes prove it), and `lookupswitch` tables are sorted by JVMS §6.5. The risk is in the review: a regression proof whose scope and bound leave it nothing to cover reads as a proof of the change, `✓ behaves as before on every input where !(matches.length <= 8)`, and a reviewer who takes the tick for the bisection's safety has been told nothing about it. A proof that says nothing must say so.
explanation: The developer declares the short tables as the intended change and asks for a proof that longer tables are searched as before. The harness compiles the scope to `if (matches.length <= 8) return;` before the calls, and the symbolic array parameter has every length up to `--max-array-length`, eight by default: every table in the domain takes the early return, neither version is ever called, and the assertion is never reached. The checker proves this in one path and no solver call, and it is a proof of nothing. The tool then runs the probe, the same harness with the two calls replaced by `throw new AssertionError()`: an input that reaches the calls would fail it, and the probe is proved too, so no input in the domain reaches the calls. The verdict stays verified, since the statement is true as stated, and the line `vacuously: no input in the domain reaches the calls, every one being among the intended inputs (--unchanged-unless); the proof covers no input and says nothing` is for the reviewer, who raises the bound (example 145) or, for the scan itself, states the scope the scan is meant to be equal under.
resolution: Do not merge on this proof. Raise the bound past the scan limit, `--max-array-length 12`, so that the domain holds tables the scope admits, which is example 145; and prove the scan equal to the bisection on the tables it is meant for, the strictly sorted ones, with the quantifier scope of example 141 (its notes).
notes: The vacuity check is the tool's, whichever engine proved the statement: the probe is run by the tool's own checker over the statement's own domain, and the line appears under a JBMC proof as it does here. It is run only when the harness skips inputs before the calls, that is with `--unchanged-unless`, a record parameter or receiver whose constructor may reject an input, or `--before-arguments` that may throw; a harness that calls the versions on every input has nothing to probe. A `prove` with `--assume` is probed the same way. The probe took 0.0 s here, one path and no solver call, since `matches.length <= 8` is a constant under the bound. Here `python3 examples/tools/build.py` compares the expected verdict with the vacuity too: an example that is verified vacuously must say so in `expected.vacuous`, as the TLC examples of [tag tla-coverage](../README.md#tag-tla-coverage) do.

Why the bound defeats the scope: the scope is over the symbolic array's length, and the domain of a regression proof over arrays is every length up to `--max-array-length`, eight by default, the same number as the scan limit. The proof line prints both, `where !(matches.length <= 8)` and `matches: int[] of length ≤ 8`, and a reader who holds them side by side sees the proof is empty; the tool now holds them side by side for the reader. A scope over the elements can be emptied the same way, by a quantifier that no array up to the bound satisfies, and a scope over scalars by an expression that is a tautology, `skewSeconds >= 0 || skewSeconds < 0`, which is what the check first caught, on example 125's method.

The scan is correct, and the proof that shows it is the one with the sortedness scope, `--unchanged-unless '!(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length - 1; matches[i] < matches[i + 1])'`: at bound eight the tool's own checker proves the new `find` equal to the old on every strictly sorted table of up to eight pairs and every key in 1.1 s, 88 paths, 660 solver calls, 46 MB, where the scan runs for every table and the bisection in the previous version; at bound twelve in 3.1 s, 180 paths, 67 MB. Without a scope the checker finds `find(matches=[20, 16], key=16)` in 0.08 s, -1 before (the bisection tests `matches[0] = 20 > 16` and moves `high` below the start) and 1 after (the scan reaches the second pair): on an unsorted table the two searches differ, as example 141 found for the half-open rewrite, and the scope states what every `lookupswitch` table satisfies.

The change is the shape of the JDK's own `DualPivotQuicksort`, which sorts small arrays by insertion sort below a constant threshold, and of many searches that scan short tables rather than bisect them: it is a performance change meant to preserve behaviour, and `behaviourChangeIntended` is false. Declaring the short tables as intended inputs is the mistake this example is about: it is the natural declaration for a reviewer who wants the bisection checked and takes the scan on trust, and it leaves the proof nothing when the bound is the threshold. The domain line of every proof names the bound for this reason.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 2 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.
provenance: Constructed on the `lookupswitch` bisection of JVMS §6.5 (examples 046, 140 and 141), with a short-table scan in the shape of the JDK's insertion-sort threshold, as the first regression-proof example of a vacuous verdict, found while adding the vacuity check to the tool.

references.title: JVMS §6.5, lookupswitch: the match-offset pairs are sorted so that an implementation may search them by bisection
OpenJDK, DualPivotQuicksort: small arrays are sorted by insertion sort, the threshold a constant of the class
Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)
Kupferman and Vardi, Vacuity detection in temporal model checking (2003)
